objectives: Tell common and proper nouns apart and use capital letters.
Use collective nouns and make simple plurals.
reviewNotes: Months are capitalised in English; collective nouns taught are the common ones; to be checked against the textbook.

blocks.title: Nouns
blocks.md: A **noun** is a **naming word**. It names a person (teacher), a place (market), an animal (goat) or a thing (book). A **common noun** names any person, place or thing: *girl, town, river*. A **proper noun** names one special person, place or thing and begins with a **capital letter**: *Ngum, Douala, River Sanaga*.

blocks.caption: Nouns name people, places, animals and things.
blocks.alt: Four boxes: person, teacher; place, Douala; animal, goat; thing, book.

blocks.title: Collective nouns
blocks.md: A **collective noun** names a group: a **class** of pupils, a **herd** of cattle, a **bunch** of bananas, a **flock** of birds, a **team** of players, a **swarm** of bees. One collective noun is one group: *The team is ready.*

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Forgetting capital letters for proper nouns: write *Bamenda*, not *bamenda*.
- Using a capital letter for common nouns in the middle of a sentence.
- Mixing up a noun with a verb: *Run* can be a verb (*I run*) or a noun (*a long run*).

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.statement: Find the nouns in: 'Ako buys a bag of rice in Bafoussam.'
steps: Look for names of people, places and things.
Ako (person, proper), bag (thing), rice (thing), Bafoussam (place, proper).

blocks.title: Example 2
blocks.statement: Fill the gap with a collective noun: a ____ of bananas.
steps: Think about how bananas grow or are sold together.
We say a bunch of bananas.

blocks.title: Pronouns
blocks.md: A **pronoun** takes the place of a noun so that we do not repeat it. *Ako is a pupil. **He** is in Class 4.* Subject pronouns: **I, you, he, she, it, we, they**. **Possessive** words show who owns something: **my, your, his, her, its, our, their**.

blocks.caption: Pronouns and possessive words.
blocks.alt: A table with the pronouns I, you, he she it, we they and the matching possessive words my, your, his her its, our their.

blocks.title: A, an and the
blocks.md: Use **a** before a consonant sound (*a book, a goat*) and **an** before a vowel sound (*an egg, an orange, an hour*). Use **the** when we speak about a particular thing we both know: *The teacher is in the classroom.*

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- *Me and Ako went home* is not correct: say *Ako and I went home*.
- *An book* is wrong: it is *a book*.
- Using *their* for one person: *Ngum lost his pen* (not *their pen*).
- Mixing *it's* (it is) and *its* (belonging to it).

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.statement: Replace the noun with a pronoun: 'Mary and Paul are in the garden. Mary and Paul are planting maize.'
steps: Mary and Paul are two people, so we use they.
Mary and Paul are in the garden. They are planting maize.

blocks.title: Example 2
blocks.statement: Choose a or an: ___ orange, ___ mango.
steps: Orange begins with a vowel sound: an orange.
Mango begins with a consonant sound: a mango.

blocks.title: Verbs
blocks.md: A **verb** is a **doing** or **being** word: *run, eat, write, is, are*. The **tense** of a verb tells **when** something happens: **present** (now or always), **past** (before now) or **future** (later). Present: *I walk.* Past: *I walked.* Future: *I will walk.*

blocks.caption: Past, present and future.
blocks.alt: A table with three columns, past present future, and the sentences I walked, I walk, I will walk, then she ate, she eats, she will eat, then they went, they go, they will go.

blocks.title: Regular and irregular verbs
blocks.md: Regular verbs add **-ed** in the past: *walk, walked; play, played*. **Irregular verbs** change in other ways: go - **went**, eat - **ate**, see - **saw**, buy - **bought**, run - **ran**, come - **came**, write - **wrote**, take - **took**. These must be learnt by heart.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Writing **goed**, **eated** or **buyed**: the past forms are *went, ate, bought*.
- Mixing tenses in one sentence: *Yesterday I go to the market* is wrong; say *Yesterday I went*.
- Using *will* with *-ed*: *I will walked* is wrong.

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.statement: Write in the past tense: 'Ako goes to school and eats bread.'
steps: The past of go is went; the past of eats is ate.
Ako went to school and ate bread.
blocks.answer: Ako went to school and ate bread.

blocks.title: Example 2
blocks.statement: Write in the future tense: 'We plant maize.'
steps: The future uses will + the simple verb.
We will plant maize.

blocks.title: Adjectives
blocks.md: An **adjective** is a **describing word**. It tells us more about a noun: a **tall** tree, a **sweet** mango, **three** goats, a **busy** market. An adjective usually goes **before** the noun or after the verb **to be**: *The road is long.*

blocks.caption: Adjectives of comparison.
blocks.alt: A table with adjectives tall, big, good and beautiful, their comparatives taller, bigger, better, more beautiful and superlatives tallest, biggest, best, most beautiful.

blocks.title: Comparing
blocks.md: To compare **two** things, add **-er** or use **more** (*Mount Cameroon is taller than the hill.*). To compare **three or more** things, add **-est** or use **most** (*It is the tallest mountain in Cameroon.*). Short words add -er/-est (doubling the last letter: big - bigger - biggest). Long words use *more/most*. Irregular: good - better - best, bad - worse - worst.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- *More taller* or *most tallest*: use only one of the two.
- *Gooder* is wrong: say *better*.
- Using *than* for the superlative: *the tallest of the three*, not *tallest than*.
- Forgetting to double the letter: *bigger*, not *biger*.

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.statement: Fill the gap: Ako is ____ than Bih. (tall)
steps: We compare two people, so we use the comparative.
Tall adds -er: taller.

blocks.title: Example 2
blocks.statement: Fill the gap: This is the ____ mango in the basket. (sweet)
steps: More than two mangoes: use the superlative.
Sweet adds -est: sweetest.

reviewNotes: 'Fast' is both an adjective and an adverb; explanation kept simple.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Adverbs
blocks.md: An **adverb** tells us more about a **verb**: **how**, **when** or **where** something happens. *She walks **slowly**. (how) We will go **tomorrow**. (when) The children play **outside**. (where)* Many adverbs of manner end in **-ly**: *quickly, carefully, loudly*.

blocks.caption: Adverbs and prepositions answer questions.
blocks.alt: Three boxes: Where, with in, on, under; When, with now, soon, often; How, with quickly, well.

blocks.title: Prepositions
blocks.md: A **preposition** shows the **position** or **time** of a noun. Place: **in** the bag, **on** the table, **under** the tree, **between** two houses, **behind** the school, **near** the river. Time: **at** 7 o'clock, **on** Monday, **in** May.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Using an adjective for an adverb: *She sings beautiful* should be *beautifully*.
- Using *in* with days: say *on Monday*, not *in Monday*.
- *Good* is an adjective, **well** is the adverb: *He plays well*.
- Confusing *at* a time and *in* a month.

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.statement: Choose the adverb: 'The teacher speaks (soft / softly).'
steps: The word describes the verb speaks, so we need an adverb.
The adverb is softly.

blocks.title: Example 2
blocks.statement: Fill the gap: 'We have English ___ Monday.'
steps: Before a day of the week we use on.
We have English on Monday.

lessons.title: Subject-verb agreement (concord)
lessons.programRef: MINEDUB primary school curriculum (English-speaking subsystem), Level II (Class 4) — English Language; to be checked against the official syllabus
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Make the verb agree with its subject.
Use is/are, was/were, has/have and does/do correctly.
Spot and correct simple concord mistakes.
reviewNotes: 'Everybody' as singular follows standard English; some speakers use a plural in speech.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Concord
blocks.md: **Concord** (agreement) means that the verb agrees with its subject. A **singular** subject takes a singular verb: *The boy **plays**.* A **plural** subject takes a plural verb: *The boys **play**.* With *he, she, it* the present verb ends in **s**: *she plays, he runs, it eats*.

items.text: Two or more: The boys play.
She / he / it: the verb takes s - plays
I / you / we / they: no s - play

blocks.caption: The verb agrees with the subject.
blocks.alt: Four stacked boxes: one person, the boy plays; two or more, the boys play; he she it takes s; I you we they take no s.

blocks.title: Is, are, has, have, was, were
blocks.md: **Is / was / has / does** go with *he, she, it* and singular nouns. **Are / were / have / do** go with *we, you, they* and plural nouns. *I* takes **am**, **was**, **have**, **do**. *There **is** a goat.* *There **are** two goats.*

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Looking at the nearest word instead of the real subject: *The box of mangoes **is** heavy*.
- *The children is playing* is wrong: *The children **are** playing*.
- *He don't know*: say *He doesn't know*.
- *Everybody are here*: *everybody* is singular (*is*).

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.statement: Choose the right word: 'The girls (sing / sings) in the choir.'
steps: The subject girls is plural.
A plural subject takes sing.

blocks.title: Example 2
steps: Ako and Bih are two people, so the subject is plural.
The verb must be are: Ako and Bih are friends.
